result: PP1 phosphatases have little intrinsic sequence specificity, and while cofactors (PIPs) can target PP1 to substrates or locations and enhance/inhibit activity, no instances of PIP-induced sequence-specificity were known prior to this study.
evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C17, C18, and C19 establish the prior state of knowledge about PP1 specificity through citations to established literature (Brautigan and Shenolikar 2018; Miller and Turk 2018; Ichikawa et al. 1996; Johnson et al. 1996). This provides essential context for the novelty of the current work.

result: Phactr1 is a neuronally enriched PP1 cofactor controlled by G-actin through RPEL motifs, with G-actin competing with PP1 for binding due to overlap of the C-terminal RPEL domain with the PP1 binding sequence, allowing rho-actin signaling to control Phactr/PP1 complex formation.
evaluation: Claims C3, C23-C28 describe established properties of Phactr proteins supported by multiple citations (Allen et al. 2004; Huet et al. 2013; Mouilleron et al. 2012; Wiezlak et al. 2012). This background information is well-documented in prior literature.

result: Phactr1 C-terminal sequences (517-580) containing the RVxF-like sequence LIRF are necessary and sufficient for PP1 binding with 10.4 nM affinity, comparable to other PIPs. Crystal structures of Phactr1/PP1 complexes were determined at 1.9-1.94 Å resolution, showing PP1 conformation virtually identical to other PP1 complexes.
evaluation: Claims C35-C41 are supported by bio-layer interferometry data (C37-C38) and high-resolution crystallographic structures (C39-C41) with appropriate controls and comparisons to published structures. The binding affinity measurements and structural data are internally consistent and well-documented.

result: Phactr1 residues 516-542 wrap around PP1 in a manner similar to spinophilin, PNUTS, and PPP1R15B, with the RVxF sequence LIRF(519-522) being critical for binding. Systematic mutagenesis revealed quantitative contributions of individual residues to binding affinity, with deletion of LIRF reducing affinity ~10,000-fold and specific mutations reducing affinity 4-fold to >300-fold.
evaluation: Claims C42-C53 are supported by structural analysis (C42-C43) and comprehensive mutagenesis data with BLI measurements (C44-C53). The mutagenesis is systematic and quantitative, with appropriate controls. The structural similarity to other PIPs is validated by RMSD calculations and citations.

result: Phactr1 binding remodels PP1's hydrophobic groove to create a novel composite surface comprising a deep hydrophobic pocket, an adjacent amphipathic cavity, and a basic rim, which radically alters PP1 surface charge distribution in a manner distinct from spinophilin/PP1.
evaluation: Claims C4, C54-C67 are supported by high-resolution structural data showing detailed molecular interactions and surface properties. Mutagenesis data (C55-C59) validate the functional importance of the identified structural features. Electrostatic surface potential calculations and comparisons with spinophilin/PP1 support the claim of distinct remodeling.

result: SILAC phosphoproteomics in NIH3T3 cells identified over 3000 phosphorylation sites, with annotation enrichment analysis revealing that Phactr1/PP1 substrates are enriched in cytoskeletal components and regulators. Sites with high dephosphorylation scores showed enrichment of acidic residues at positions +2 to +7 and hydrophobic residues at +4/+5.
evaluation: Claims C70-C73, C5 are supported by comprehensive SILAC phosphoproteomics data with appropriate controls (Phactr1XXX vs Phactr1XXXΔC and vector). Annotation enrichment analysis using established methods (Cox and Mann 2012) identified statistically significant GO categories. Sequence analysis revealed clear positional preferences.

result: In vitro phosphatase assays revealed that candidate substrates exhibit a range of kinetic parameters, with IRSp53 pS455 showing low KM and high kcat/KM. The four substrates with lowest KM (IRSp53 pS455, Plekho2 pS395, spectrin αII pS1031, Tbc1d15 pS205) all contained a leucine doublet at positions +4/+5.
evaluation: Claims C74-C77 are supported by systematic in vitro phosphatase assays with quantitative kinetic measurements. The correlation between leucine doublets and low KM is based on direct observation across multiple substrates, though the mechanistic basis is explained by subsequent structural studies.

result: Phosphorylation of IRSp53 S455 and afadin S1275 was substantially decreased by Phactr1XXX expression and serum stimulation in NIH3T3 cells. Treatment with cytochalasin D (which disrupts G-actin-RPEL interaction) decreased phosphorylation, while latrunculin B (which increases G-actin but doesn't disrupt RPEL binding) increased phosphorylation.
evaluation: Claims C78-C81 are supported by immunoblot data with phospho-specific antibodies and appropriate pharmacological controls. The opposing effects of CD and LB are consistent with the model that G-actin-Phactr binding regulates PP1 complex formation. Quantitation is provided in Supplementary file 3.

result: Phactr1-null mice are viable without obvious developmental abnormalities and with unaffected expression of other Phactr proteins. TMT phosphoproteomics in neurons identified 44 sites on 37 proteins that differed significantly in their response to CD/LB stimuli in Phactr1-null cells, with seven sites (including IRSp53 pS455, spectrin αII pS1031, afadin pS1275) observed in both NIH3T3 cells and neurons.
evaluation: Claims C84-C87 are supported by RT-PCR data (C85) and TMT phosphoproteomics with appropriate statistical analysis (C86). The overlap between cell types (C87) strengthens the identification of bona fide substrates. However, the viability of Phactr1-null mice (C84) suggests potential compensation by other Phactr family members.

result: High-resolution structures of Phactr1/PP1 bound to IRSp53(449-465) and spectrin αII(1025-1039) were determined at 1.09 Å and 1.30 Å resolution using PP1-substrate fusion proteins. The complexes contain phosphate at the catalytic site and appear to represent enzyme-product complexes, with substrate sequences making extensive contacts across the PP1 catalytic site and the composite Phactr1/PP1 surface.
evaluation: Claims C88-C94 are supported by high-resolution crystallographic data with excellent statistics (Table 1). The fusion protein strategy is well-justified and analogous to published PP5 work (Oberoi et al. 2016). The structures show clear electron density for substrates and phosphate, supporting the enzyme-product complex interpretation.

result: The phosphate is inverted in substrate complexes compared to the holoenzyme, with a bound water (W1) positioned for in-line nucleophilic attack on the substrate phosphate. This inversion provides direct evidence for the in-line nucleophilic hydrolysis mechanism proposed for PPP family phosphatases.
evaluation: Claims C95, C7, C98-C102, C137 are supported by high-resolution structural data showing phosphate positions in both holoenzyme and product complexes. The interpretation is consistent with established mechanistic proposals (Egloff et al. 1995; Swingle et al. 2004) and comparison with the PP5/Cdc37(S13E) structure. This represents strong structural evidence for the catalytic mechanism.

result: Substrate sequences C-terminal to the dephosphorylation site make intimate contacts with the composite Phactr1/PP1 surface, with the hydrophobic doublet L459-L460 (IRSp53) or L1035-L1036 (spectrin) at positions +4/+5 making critical contacts with the hydrophobic pocket. Mutagenesis showed these interactions are required for efficient dephosphorylation both in vitro and in vivo.
evaluation: Claims C8, C103-C108 are supported by structural data showing detailed substrate-enzyme contacts and systematic mutagenesis with both in vitro kinetic measurements and cellular validation. The LL459/460AA mutant being essentially unreactive (C106) and IRSp53(L460A) showing enhanced basal phosphorylation in cells (C107) provide strong functional validation.

result: Peptide overlay assays showed that only low KM substrates (IRSp53, spectrin αII, Tbc1d15, Plekho2) exhibited detectable binding. Peptide array analysis revealed that positions +4 and +5 displayed the strongest selectivity for hydrophobic residues and leucine, respectively, with phenylalanine substitution at IRSp53 L459 (+4) increasing both binding affinity and catalytic efficiency.
evaluation: Claims C109-C112 are supported by peptide overlay assays and systematic peptide array data. The correlation between binding affinity and KM is logical, and the enhancement by F459 substitution (C111) provides functional validation. The comprehensive mutagenesis across all positions strengthens the conclusions about specificity determinants.

result: In the Phactr1/PP1-IRSp53(S455E) phosphomimetic complex, T456 occupies the position of S455 in the wildtype complex, with the glutamate at position -1. Critical contacts with the hydrophobic pocket are maintained. Both IRSp53 pT456 and E455/pT456 were effective substrates with only 2-fold lower catalytic efficiency, while pS453 and pS454 were very poor substrates, indicating that substrates can tolerate 3 or 4 residues between the target and the hydrophobic pocket.
evaluation: Claims C113-C117 are supported by a 1.39 Å structure of the S455E complex and kinetic data for alternative phosphorylation sites. The structural observation that the substrate can shift register while maintaining pocket contacts (C113-C114) is directly validated by the kinetic data showing T456 is an effective substrate (C115). This demonstrates flexibility in the recognition mechanism.

result: Phactr1/PP1 exhibits 100-400-fold greater catalytic efficiency toward its substrates (IRSp53 pS455, CD2ap pS458, afadin pS1275) compared to apo-PP1 or spinophilin/PP1. However, cofilin pS3 showed only 2-fold enhancement. Phactr1 did not enhance activity against glycogen phosphorylase pS15 or GluR1 pS863. A PP1-Phactr1 fusion protein behaved similarly, indicating RVxF interactions are not essential for specificity.
evaluation: Claims C9, C31, C34, C118-C122 are supported by comprehensive comparative phosphatase assays with multiple substrates and enzyme forms. The differential enhancement (100-400-fold for good substrates vs 2-fold for cofilin) and lack of activity against non-substrates demonstrates genuine sequence specificity. The fusion protein control (C121) validates that the composite surface, not just RVxF binding, confers specificity.

result: Efficient catalysis requires interactions between conserved hydrophobic residues in substrates and the novel Phactr1-PP1 composite surface (hydrophobic pocket, amphipathic cavity, basic rim). Phactr/PP1 substrates can be defined by a core recognition sequence S/T-x(2-3)-ϕ-L, with a hydrophobic doublet at +4/+5 or +3/+4 and leucine preferred at the distal position, embedded in acidic sequences. This is perhaps the first identified sequence specificity motif for PP1.
evaluation: Claims C32-C33, C123, C144-C145 synthesize structural, kinetic, and binding data to define a consensus sequence. The proposal is well-supported by multiple lines of evidence: structural contacts, mutagenesis, peptide arrays, and kinetic measurements. The comparison to kinase recognition sequences (C145) is appropriate, though the claim of being 'the first' for PP1 should be qualified by the lack of prior systematic studies.

result: Phactr1/PP1 dephosphorylates multiple cytoskeletal proteins and regulators identified by phosphoproteomics. Substrates include IRSp53 (a Cdc42/Rac effector) at pS455 and pS367 (14-3-3 binding sites), spectrin αII and girdin at sites adjacent to SH3/SH2 domains, and the actin depolymerizing factors cofilin and destrin.
evaluation: Claims C125-C130 are supported by phosphoproteomics data and citations to prior functional studies. The identification of specific sites (C127-C128) is validated by multiple approaches. The functional context provided by citations (Cohen et al. 2011; Kast and Dominguez 2019; Huet et al. 2013) strengthens the biological significance.

result: Phactr1 is enriched at the post-synaptic density and required for neuronal migration and arborization. Several Phactr1-dependent substrates (IRSp53, spectrin αII) are dephosphorylated during LTP, and IRSp53-null mice exhibit deficits in hippocampal learning and memory. Cofilin dephosphorylation is implicated in dendritic spine remodeling. In humans, Phactr1 mutations cause West syndrome.
evaluation: Claims C131-C136 are supported by citations to published studies (Allen et al. 2004; Hamada et al. 2018; Li et al. 2016; Bobsin and Kreienkamp 2016; Kang et al. 2016; Bosch et al. 2014; Lei et al. 2017). These claims establish the neurobiological context and significance of the findings, though they represent prior work rather than new results from this study.

result: The majority of PP1 catalytic cleft residues contacting substrates are conserved among PPP family members including PP5. Surprisingly, Phactr1/PP1 substrates dock in the opposite orientation to that seen in the PP5/Cdc37(S13E) complex, despite analogous contacts by conserved residues.
evaluation: Claims C96-C97, C138 are supported by structural comparisons with the PP5/Cdc37(S13E) structure (Oberoi et al. 2016) and sequence conservation analysis. The opposite orientation is clearly documented in Figure 4—figure supplement 2. This observation raises interesting questions about substrate recognition diversity in the PPP family.

result: The additional binding energy from substrate interactions with the hydrophobic pocket is proposed to be responsible for enhanced catalytic rate. Substrates with higher KM might be more promiscuous in their PP1 complex interactions (exemplified by cofilin pS3), while high binding affinities might limit catalytic efficiency by slowing product dissociation (possibly exemplified by spectrin).
evaluation: Claims C139-C142 represent mechanistic interpretations and speculations based on the kinetic data. While the general principle that binding energy enhances catalysis is sound (C139), the specific proposals about promiscuity (C140-C141) and product dissociation (C142) are speculative and would require additional experiments (e.g., product release measurements, competition assays) to validate.

result: Targeting the composite Phactr1/PP1 surface may be a good strategy for creating specific Phactr/PP1 inhibitors. Mutation of positions +4/+5 in candidate substrates will be useful for generating constitutively phosphorylated mutants for functional studies.
evaluation: Claims C143 and C146 represent reasonable proposals based on the findings. C143 is supported by the demonstration that the composite surface confers specificity and citation to the lack of specificity in current PP1 inhibitors (Zhang et al. 2013). C146 is validated by the demonstration that L460A mutation increases basal phosphorylation in cells (C107).

result: Spinophilin remodels the PP1 hydrophobic groove differently than Phactr1 and does not enhance PP1 activity toward Phactr/PP1 substrates. MYPT interacts with PP1 differently, extending both C-terminal and acidic grooves. PIPs constrain specificity by occluding PP1 surfaces. Phactr-family members lack conserved autonomous substrate-binding domains seen in other PIPs.
evaluation: Claims C147-C151 are supported by structural comparisons (C147, C149), biochemical data (C148), and sequence analysis (C151), all with appropriate citations. These comparisons contextualize the Phactr1/PP1 mechanism within the broader landscape of PP1 regulation and highlight its unique features.

result: Many PIPs target PP1 to specific subcellular locations. Phactr-family proteins exhibit differential subcellular localizations and Phactr1 interacts with the KCNT1 potassium channel. Membrane targeting involves conserved N-terminal sequences. The genetic dominance of Phactr mutations suggests interactions with other cellular components beyond PP1. The range of substrates controlled by Phactr1/PP1 will reflect cellular actin dynamics, subcellular localization, and direct sequence recognition.
evaluation: Claims C152-C157 are supported by citations to published work and represent reasonable integration of the findings with prior knowledge. C157 is a well-reasoned synthesis acknowledging that substrate specificity in cells depends on multiple factors beyond the intrinsic sequence recognition demonstrated here.

result: Expression of activated Phactr1 derivatives (Phactr1XXX or the PP1-binding domain alone) induces F-actin rearrangements in NIH3T3 fibroblasts and morphological defects in cultured hippocampal neurons. Phactr1 mutations are associated with morphological and functional developmental defects in cortical neurons.
evaluation: Claims C68-C69, C82-C83 are supported by citations to prior work (Wiezlak et al. 2012; Hamada et al. 2018) and data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and 3—figure supplement 2A. These observations establish the functional consequences of Phactr1/PP1 activity and provide biological context for the substrate identification studies.

result: The overlap of the RVxF motif with RPEL3 explains why G-actin competes with PP1 to bind Phactr1 and Phactr4, allowing Phactr1/PP1 complex formation to be controlled by fluctuations in actin dynamics.
evaluation: Claim C124 is supported by structural data showing the overlap (C48-C49) and citations to prior functional studies (Huet et al. 2013; Wiezlak et al. 2012). This represents an important mechanistic insight into how actin dynamics regulate Phactr1/PP1 activity, integrating structural and functional data.
